sections.title: Introduction
sections.text:
Welcome. Today's story is one of the most dramatic in the whole Bible. It has jealousy and betrayal, slavery and prison, dreams and famine, and finally a family reunion full of tears. It is the story of Joseph, found in Genesis chapters thirty-seven through fifty.

Joseph was the great-grandson of Abraham. His life shows us that God is at work even in the worst moments — even when people hurt us, and even when it seems like God has forgotten us. As you listen, think about a time when life felt unfair. What might God have been doing that you couldn't see?

sections.title: The Story, Part 1
sections.text:
Joseph's father was Jacob, who was also called Israel. Jacob had twelve sons, but he loved Joseph most. Genesis chapter thirty-seven, verse three says: “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours.”

That coat was a constant reminder to Joseph's brothers that he was the favorite, and they hated him for it. Then Joseph had two dreams. In the first, he and his brothers were binding sheaves of grain in the field, and their sheaves bowed down to his. In the second, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowed down to him. When Joseph told his family these dreams, his brothers hated him even more.

One day Jacob sent Joseph to check on his brothers, who were feeding the flocks far from home. When they saw him coming, they said, “Behold, this dreamer cometh.” They plotted to kill him. Reuben, the oldest, convinced them to throw him into a pit instead, intending to rescue him later. They stripped off his coat and threw him into an empty pit. Then, while they sat down to eat, a caravan of traders came by on the way to Egypt. Judah said, why kill him? Let's sell him. So they sold their brother for twenty pieces of silver.

They dipped Joseph's coat in the blood of a goat and brought it to their father. Jacob recognized it and cried, “an evil beast hath devoured him.” He tore his clothes and mourned for his son for many days, and refused to be comforted.

sections.title: The Story, Part 2
sections.text:
In Egypt, Joseph was sold to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. And here the Bible repeats a phrase we need to notice: “And the LORD was with Joseph.” Joseph worked hard and faithfully, and God blessed everything he did, until Potiphar put him in charge of his whole house.

But Potiphar's wife tried again and again to tempt Joseph. He refused, saying, “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Angry at being refused, she falsely accused him, and Joseph was thrown into prison. Yet even there, the Bible says, the Lord was with Joseph, and the prison keeper put him in charge of the other prisoners.

In prison, Joseph interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's chief butler and chief baker. Everything happened just as Joseph said. The butler was restored to his job — but he forgot all about Joseph. Two more full years passed.

Then Pharaoh had two troubling dreams that no one could explain. Finally the butler remembered Joseph. Joseph was brought out of prison, shaved, given clean clothes, and brought before the most powerful man in the world. Pharaoh said he had heard that Joseph could interpret dreams. Joseph answered humbly, in Genesis chapter forty-one, verse sixteen: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.”

God revealed the meaning: seven years of great plenty were coming, followed by seven years of severe famine. Joseph advised Pharaoh to store up grain during the good years. Pharaoh was so impressed that he put Joseph in charge of all the land of Egypt. At thirty years old, the former slave and prisoner was second only to Pharaoh.

When the famine came, it reached Canaan too, and Jacob sent his sons to Egypt to buy grain. They came and bowed before the governor — not knowing it was Joseph. His dreams had come true. After testing them to see if they had changed, Joseph could hold back no longer. He sent everyone else out of the room and wept so loudly that the Egyptians heard. He said, “I am Joseph.” His brothers were terrified. But Joseph forgave them, and he brought his father and the whole family to live in Egypt.

Years later, after Jacob died, the brothers worried that Joseph would finally take revenge. But Joseph said, in Genesis chapter fifty, verse twenty: “But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.”

sections.title: The Lesson
sections.text:
What do we learn from Joseph?

First, God is present in the pit and in the prison. Joseph's circumstances went from bad to worse, but four words kept repeating: the Lord was with Joseph. Your hard season does not mean God has left you.

Second, faithfulness in small places matters. Whether Joseph was a slave in a house or a prisoner in a jail, he did his work with excellence and integrity. He didn't wait for better circumstances to do his best.

Third, God can use what was meant for evil and turn it to good. That doesn't make the evil good. What Joseph's brothers did was wrong. But God was bigger than their sin, and He used even their betrayal to save many lives.

And finally, forgiveness is possible. Joseph had every reason and every opportunity to take revenge. Instead, he chose to forgive. Forgiveness doesn't pretend the hurt never happened. It trusts God with the hurt and chooses not to repay evil for evil.

sections.title: Prayer and Reflection
sections.text:
Is there someone who has hurt you that you are finding it hard to forgive? Or a hard situation where you are wondering if God is still with you? Take a moment and bring that to God now.

Let's pray. Lord, thank You that You were with Joseph, and that You are with me, even in the hard places. Help me to be faithful where I am today. Give me a heart that forgives, the way You have forgiven me. And help me trust that You can bring good even out of what hurts. In Jesus' name, Amen.

Thank you for listening. Next time, we'll hear how God used Moses to lead His people out of slavery in Egypt.
